title: Framework vs Library
griotIntro: At the great fair of Louga, you choose for yourself which merchant to approach — you decide the path.
A library works the same way: you're the one who calls it. A framework, on the other hand, imposes its own path and calls you when IT decides to.

explanation.text: The real distinction isn't the size of the code, but who controls the flow of execution — this is called inversion of control. Click on the lines to see the difference.

annotations.note: You decide when to call `formatDate` — your code is driving, the library just waits to be called.
You write `MyComponent`, but you never call it yourself — React decides when to render it, re-render it, or destroy it.
This is inversion of control: with a framework, IT holds the thread of execution, your code slots into ITS structure.
Even a custom hook (`useXxx`) remains a function that React must call itself according to its own rules — reusable logic never fully escapes inversion of control.

lines: // We want to reuse the logic without going through React
const value = Counter(); // direct call of the component function
bugHunt.explanation: Counter is a React component, not an ordinary function: calling it directly breaks the rules of hooks, because `useState` must be invoked by React itself, within the context of a render managed by the framework. This is inversion of control in action — React must call `Counter()`, never your own code. To reuse this logic outside of a component, you need to extract a custom hook (e.g. `useCounter`) and call it from a real component.

useCases: Choosing lodash or date-fns (libraries) for one-off utilities, without imposing structure on the rest of the project.
Choosing React, Angular, or NestJS (frameworks) to structure an entire application according to imposed conventions.
Express sits between the two: it structures HTTP routes but remains much more permissive than a framework like NestJS.

relatedTools.name: date-fns / lodash
relatedTools.description: Classic utility libraries: you import only the functions you need, with no structural constraints.

relatedTools.name: React / Angular / NestJS
relatedTools.description: Frameworks that impose their own lifecycle and conventions — code is written "inside" their structure.

relatedTools.name: Express
relatedTools.description: Often called a "micro-framework": it structures HTTP routing but leaves everything else completely free, unlike NestJS.

practice.question: Why is Express said to be closer to a library than NestJS?
options: Express lets developers organize their project however they want, while NestJS imposes a precise structure (modules, decorators)
Express is newer than NestJS
Express cannot handle HTTP routes

feedback.correct: Exactly — the library/framework spectrum isn't binary, Express sits between the two.
feedback.incorrect: The key difference is the degree of structural constraint imposed, not age or routing features.

quiz.question: What is the fundamental difference between a library and a framework?
options: Who controls the flow of execution: you (library) or it (framework, inversion of control)
A library is always smaller in code size
A framework can never be used partially

quiz.question: What is "inversion of control"?
options: The framework calls your code according to ITS own rules, rather than your code calling the framework
A principle that only exists in object-oriented programming
Reversing the order of unit tests

quiz.question: Can a library easily be replaced in a project?
options: Generally yes, because it doesn't impose a global structure on the rest of the code
Never, a library is just as constraining as a framework
Only if the project has a single file

quiz.question: Why is switching frameworks mid-project generally more costly than switching libraries?
options: Because the code is written "inside" the framework's conventions, not just connected to it
Because frameworks are always paid
It's never more costly, that's a myth

quiz.question: In an interview, how would you justify choosing a library over a framework for a small utility script?
options: A framework would add structure and a learning curve disproportionate to a one-off, isolated need
Frameworks are always forbidden for small scripts
Libraries are always faster at runtime, without exception

quiz.question: A developer claims a library can never become large or complex, unlike a framework. What do you think?
options: That's false: the size and complexity of the code don't define the library/framework distinction, only control of the execution flow matters
That's true, a library always stays small by definition
That's true only for libraries written in JavaScript

quiz.question: Why is code written with a simple library often easier to test than a component tightly coupled to a framework's lifecycle?
options: Because you call the library's functions yourself in isolation, whereas a component driven by the framework often depends on a runtime environment that needs to be simulated
Because frameworks technically cannot be tested at all
Because libraries never have bugs, unlike frameworks

culture: The debate "is React a framework or a library" comes up regularly in the JS community: React officially presents itself as a "library" (for the UI only), but its ecosystem (React Router, hooks, component lifecycle) makes it work like a framework in practice — the line is sometimes more a matter of marketing than strict definition.

pionnier.portrait: British software engineer and author, long-time Chief Scientist at ThoughtWorks, known for having formalized many software architecture concepts widely adopted by the industry.
pionnier.contribution: In an influential 2004 article ("Inversion of Control Containers and the Dependency Injection pattern"), he clarified and popularized the term "inversion of control," which has since become the reference criterion for distinguishing a framework from a library.
pionnier.problematique: Developers used the terms "framework" and "library" confusingly, with no clear criterion to distinguish them beyond code size or complexity.
pionnier.solution: He proposed defining the distinction by who holds control of the execution flow: the calling code (library) or the called code (framework, via inversion of control).
pionnier.resultat: This criterion is now taught and cited in nearly all resources and technical interviews dealing with this topic, far beyond his original article.

ambiguite.question: Is React a framework or a library?
ambiguite.reponse: Officially a library (it only handles display), but in practice it largely imposes its own way of structuring an application (components, state, lifecycle) to the point where many developers consider it a framework. It's a good example that this boundary isn't always clear-cut.

title: React, Vue, Angular: Compared Cultures
griotIntro: Three different caravans can all take you to Louga — each with its own pace and its own rules of travel.
React, Vue, and Angular solve the same problem (building interfaces) with very different philosophies.

explanation.text: The three most widely used frontend frameworks have distinct philosophies: React leaves the most freedom (just a view library + JSX), Angular imposes the most structure (TypeScript, dependency injection), Vue aims for an accessible compromise. Click on the lines to compare the same component.

annotations.note: React mixes JS logic and display structure (JSX) in a single function — flexible, but requires personal discipline to stay readable.
Vue separates the template (declarative HTML) from logic — a syntax designed to be readable even without much JS experience.
Angular imposes classes, decorators, and TypeScript by default — more imposed structure, more guardrails, but a steeper learning curve.
Angular natively offers two-way binding via `ngModel` — the view can modify the data AND automatically push it back into the component, while React and Vue remain unidirectional data flow by default.

bugHunt.explanation: React compares the old and new state reference to decide whether to re-render the component. `items.push(newItem)` mutates the existing array in place: `items` therefore keeps the same reference, and `setItems(items)` triggers no re-render since React detects no change. You need to create a new array, for example `setItems([...items, newItem])`, to respect the immutability expected by React (unlike Vue, whose reactivity system directly detects mutation of a proxied array).

useCases: React for a startup that wants to iterate fast with a wide choice of third-party libraries, with no imposed structure.
Angular for a large company that wants strict, consistent structure across dozens of different teams.
Vue for a team that wants a gentle learning curve, often chosen for gradual migrations of an existing site.

relatedTools.name: Next.js
relatedTools.description: Framework built on top of React that adds routing, server-side rendering, and much more — illustrates how the React ecosystem organizes itself in layers.

relatedTools.name: Nuxt
relatedTools.description: The Vue equivalent of Next.js — the same "framework on top of" a view library logic.

relatedTools.name: Angular CLI
relatedTools.description: Angular natively includes its own command-line tool for generating components, services, and tests — a strong cultural difference from React/Vue, which delegate this to the ecosystem.

practice.question: Which statement best describes Angular's philosophy compared to React?
options: Angular imposes a complete structure (TypeScript, dependency injection, official CLI), while React leaves most choices to the ecosystem
Angular and React are interchangeable with no difference in philosophy
React imposes more structure than Angular

feedback.correct: Exactly — this is the most cited distinction in frontend interviews.
feedback.incorrect: It's the opposite: Angular is the most structured and prescriptive of the three, React the most permissive.

quiz.question: Which framework imposes TypeScript and a module-based architecture by default?
options: Angular
React
jQuery

quiz.question: What is JSX, used by React?
options: A syntax extension that lets you write HTML directly inside JavaScript
A new programming language independent of JavaScript
A configuration file format

quiz.question: Why would a company with many teams choose Angular over React?
options: The structure imposed by Angular reduces style divergence between different teams
Angular is always faster at runtime than React
React cannot be used by multiple teams at the same time

quiz.question: Vue is often described as a compromise between React and Angular. Why?
options: It offers an accessible declarative syntax like Angular, while staying lighter and more flexible like React
Vue literally combines the source code of React and Angular
Vue has actually no difference from the other two

quiz.question: In an interview, what is the best answer to "which frontend framework is the best"?
options: It depends on context: team size, need for structure, existing ecosystem, acceptable learning curve
React is always objectively the best choice, without exception
Angular is obsolete and should never be used again

quiz.question: Which statement correctly describes the difference between React's Virtual DOM and Vue's reactivity system?
options: React recalculates and diffs a virtual tree on every render to determine changes, while Vue precisely tracks which reactive properties changed thanks to its dependency system, without rebuilding the whole tree
React and Vue use exactly the same Virtual DOM mechanism, with no difference at all
Vue has no change-tracking mechanism at all: it re-renders the entire DOM on every change

quiz.question: Why can the strict typing imposed by Angular (TypeScript by default) be seen as both an advantage and a drawback in an interview?
options: It brings more safety and compile-time error detection, but adds weight to the learning curve and code for small projects
TypeScript always makes code slower at runtime, with no benefit at all
Angular actually never imposes TypeScript, that's a common myth

culture: The "frontend framework wars" have been a classic of dev culture since 2014 (AngularJS then Angular vs React vs Vue) — sometimes very passionate debates on social media, whereas in practice most senior engineers consider that the choice matters less than the quality of execution with the tool chosen.

pionnier.portrait: Software engineer at Facebook, creator of React, publicly unveiled in 2013 after first being used internally on Facebook's News Feed.
pionnier.contribution: He designed React and its Virtual DOM, an approach that has durably influenced how the industry builds complex, reactive user interfaces.
pionnier.problematique: On complex interfaces with many frequent updates, directly manipulating the browser DOM on every state change became costly in performance and hard to maintain consistently.
pionnier.solution: He proposed representing the interface as a lightweight virtual tree in memory (the Virtual DOM), which React compares to the previous state to compute and apply to the real DOM only the strictly necessary changes.
pionnier.resultat: React became one of the most widely used frontend libraries in the world, and its model (components, state, Virtual DOM) has directly or indirectly inspired a large share of the frontend frameworks that have appeared since.

ambiguite.question: Are AngularJS and Angular the same framework?
ambiguite.reponse: No, despite the very similar name: AngularJS (2010) is the old version, entirely rewritten in 2016 under the name "Angular" (sometimes called Angular 2+), with a completely different architecture (TypeScript, components). These are not versions of the same framework but two distinct frameworks that share a lineage.

title: Node.js, Deno, Bun: JavaScript Runtimes
griotIntro: Three different vehicles can get you across the same road between Louga and Dakar, but not at the same speed nor with the same comfort.
Node.js, Deno, and Bun all run JavaScript on the server side — with very different choices about security, speed, and built-in tools.

explanation.text: Node.js remains the historical standard and the most used in enterprise; Deno and Bun were born to fix design choices in Node considered outdated. Click on the lines to see the same simple task on the three runtimes.

annotations.note: Node.js accesses the file system without asking for any special permission — convenient, but malicious code has the same access as any other code.
Deno denies all access (files, network) without explicit permission granted at launch — a secure-by-default choice, the opposite of Node.
Bun aims for compatibility with the existing Node API (`fs`, `require`) while being a rewritten runtime built to be much faster, with a bundler and package manager built in.
`import.meta.url` works natively on Deno and Bun with no extra configuration, whereas Node.js long required workarounds for this kind of module metadata in a CommonJS environment.

bugHunt.explanation: Deno denies all network access by default: running the script with `deno run script.ts` without permission will cause an error at the `fetch` call, since no network permission was granted. You need to explicitly allow it with `deno run --allow-net script.ts`, in line with Deno's explicit-permission security model — unlike Node.js, which would have run this same fetch without asking anything.

useCases: Node.js for an enterprise project that needs the widest and most mature npm ecosystem on the market.
Deno for a script or service where security by default (explicit permissions) is a real requirement, or to enjoy native TypeScript support with no configuration.
Bun to speed up build/startup times of an existing Node project, often adopted as a near-direct replacement.

relatedTools.name: npm / pnpm / yarn
relatedTools.description: Package managers of the Node ecosystem — Bun includes its own compatible package manager, much faster.

relatedTools.name: Express / Fastify (Node.js)
relatedTools.description: HTTP frameworks historically designed for Node.js, now largely compatible with Bun thanks to its API compatibility.

relatedTools.name: Fresh (Deno)
relatedTools.description: Native web framework for Deno, designed to take advantage of the runtime's native security and TypeScript support.

practice.question: What is the difference in security philosophy between Node.js and Deno?
options: Node.js allows all system access by default; Deno requires explicit permissions (--allow-read, --allow-net...)
Deno and Node.js have exactly the same security model
Node.js is actually more restrictive than Deno

feedback.correct: Exactly — this is the most cited design argument for Deno.
feedback.incorrect: It's the opposite: Deno was created in part to fix Node.js's default free system access.

quiz.question: Who created Node.js and Deno?
options: The same person, Ryan Dahl, with Deno being in part a response to choices he regretted in Node
Two completely independent teams with no connection at all
Deno was created well before Node.js

quiz.question: What is Bun's main selling point?
options: Execution and startup speed, with a runtime, bundler, and package manager combined into a single tool
Security through explicit permissions
The impossibility of using JavaScript, only TypeScript

quiz.question: Why does the maturity of the npm ecosystem remain a strong argument in favor of Node.js?
options: Millions of libraries tested in production for over 10 years, unmatched compatibility and documentation
npm only works with Node.js, no other runtime can use it at all
It's no longer a valid argument today, npm has been abandoned

quiz.question: Can an existing Node.js project migrate to Bun without a complete rewrite?
options: Often yes, thanks to the API compatibility Bun aims for with Node.js, with occasional adjustments
Never, Bun uses a language completely different from JavaScript
Only if the project uses no npm dependencies at all

quiz.question: In an interview, what factor should weigh most heavily when choosing a runtime for a new enterprise project?
options: The maturity of the ecosystem, long-term support, and the expertise already present in the team — not just raw speed benchmarks
Only the raw performance benchmarks published by each runtime
The newest runtime is always the best choice for any project

quiz.question: In what case would Deno be a BAD choice despite its security advantages?
options: For an existing enterprise project heavily dependent on native npm packages (C++ bindings) whose compatibility with the Deno ecosystem isn't guaranteed
Deno never has a bad use case, it replaces Node.js in absolutely every situation
Deno is a bad choice only for scripts under 10 lines

quiz.question: Does Deno's native TypeScript support mean there's never a need for a build step anymore?
options: For simple execution, yes, but a complex project (bundling, multiple compatibility targets) may still require extra build steps
Yes, absolutely no build configuration is ever needed with Deno, whatever the project
No, in reality Deno doesn't natively support TypeScript

culture: Ryan Dahl, creator of Node.js, gave a famous talk in 2018 ("10 Things I Regret About Node.js") in which he criticizes his own initial design choices — Deno was born directly from that self-criticism. It's a fairly rare example in tech of a creator publicly revisiting their own work to propose a better version of it.

pionnier.portrait: Developer who created Node.js in 2009, presented at JSConf Berlin that same year, then creator of Deno, announced in 2018 at JSConf EU.
pionnier.contribution: He made it possible to run JavaScript server-side with an efficient non-blocking I/O model, then designed a second runtime to fix choices he regretted in his first creation.
pionnier.problematique: At the time, efficiently handling many simultaneous network connections server-side was difficult with the dominant languages and models, often blocking on I/O operations.
pionnier.solution: He built Node.js on Chrome's V8 engine with an event loop and non-blocking I/O, allowing many connections to be handled with few resources; years later, he created Deno to introduce by default an explicit-permission security model and native TypeScript support.
pionnier.resultat: Node.js became one of the most widely used server runtimes in the world, at the base of a huge ecosystem (npm); Deno then influenced the thinking of an entire industry on default security in JavaScript runtimes.

ambiguite.question: Is Bun just a competitor to Node.js, or something different?
ambiguite.reponse: Bun is both a JavaScript runtime (like Node.js) AND a bundler, a package manager, and a test runner, all combined into a single binary. Node.js, on the other hand, has historically delegated these functions to separate tools (webpack, npm, Jest) — so the comparison isn't entirely "apples to apples".

title: Bundlers: Vite, Webpack, esbuild
griotIntro: Before heading to the fair, one carefully gathers and packs all the goods scattered around the house.
A bundler does the same with your code: it gathers dozens of scattered JS/CSS files into a package optimized for the browser.

explanation.text: A bundler solves a concrete problem: browsers load hundreds of small separate files slowly. It combines them, optimizes them, and allows the use of modern features (import/export, JSX, TypeScript) that the browser doesn't understand natively. Click on the lines to see what happens before/after bundling.

annotations.note: The browser would need to load THIS file separately — one more network request, a slower load.
`import`/`export` are modern syntax: older browsers or some environments don't understand it natively without a bundler.
The bundler merged the two files into one, removed the now-unnecessary imports/exports, and often minified the code to reduce its size.
Dynamic import lets the bundler create a separate bundle ("chunk") loaded only when that code is actually needed — this is code splitting, a complement to classic bundling.

lines: export function heavyUnusedHelper() { /* very large function, never used */ }
bugHunt.explanation: Importing the whole module with `import * as utils` often prevents the bundler from excluding unused functions like `heavyUnusedHelper`, even if only one function (`debounce`) is actually consumed in the file. Tree-shaking works much better with explicit named imports, for example `import { debounce } from './utils.js'`, which let the bundler precisely identify what's used and eliminate the rest at build time.

useCases: Vite for a new modern frontend project: near-instant startup in development thanks to using the browser's native ES modules.
Webpack for an existing project with a complex configuration already in place and many specific plugins.
esbuild for ultra-fast bundling needs, often used internally BY other tools (Vite itself uses it for certain steps).

relatedTools.name: Vite (used in this project)
relatedTools.description: Modern bundler that serves code with almost no transformation in development, and optimizes only at final build time — hence its speed.

relatedTools.name: Webpack
relatedTools.description: The historical bundler most used for years, highly configurable but known to be slower and more complex to configure than Vite.

relatedTools.name: esbuild / SWC
relatedTools.description: Bundlers/transpilers written in compiled languages (Go, Rust) rather than JavaScript, which makes them much faster — often used as the internal engine of other tools.

practice.question: Why is Vite reputed to be faster than Webpack in development?
options: Vite serves code with almost no transformation in development (native ES modules), it only truly bundles at final build time
Vite never performs any code transformation, even in production
Webpack was never designed to work with React

feedback.correct: Exactly — this is the key architectural difference between the two tools.
feedback.incorrect: Vite does optimize code well at build time, but avoids that heavy work during development to stay fast.

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of a bundler?
options: Combine several JS/CSS files into an optimized set, understandable by all browsers
Completely replace the need to write JavaScript
Host the application in production

quiz.question: Why do we need to transform JSX or TypeScript before sending them to the browser?
options: Browsers natively understand neither JSX nor TypeScript, only standard JavaScript
JSX and TypeScript run faster without transformation
It's never necessary, all browsers understand them natively

quiz.question: What is minification performed by a bundler?
options: Reducing code size (shortened variable names, removed whitespace) without changing its behavior
Removing features from the code to simplify it
Translating the code into another programming language

quiz.question: Why is esbuild so fast compared to historical bundlers written in JavaScript?
options: It's written in Go, a compiled language, whereas historical bundlers run on the JavaScript engine itself
It actually does no work at all, just copies files
It only exists for very small projects

quiz.question: In an interview, how would you justify migrating an old Webpack project to Vite?
options: A real gain in development speed and configuration simplicity, to be weighed against migration cost and the already-stable existing Webpack configuration
You must always migrate systematically, without ever evaluating migration cost
Webpack has not worked at all since 2023

quiz.question: A team imports a single function with `import { debounce } from 'lodash'` and expects tree-shaking to automatically eliminate the rest of lodash's code at build time. What pitfall explains why this isn't always the case?
options: Tree-shaking depends on the module format (ESM vs CommonJS) and the absence of declared side effects — a library distributed as classic CommonJS like lodash doesn't allow fine-grained elimination without using a variant like `lodash-es` or a targeted import (`lodash/debounce`)
Tree-shaking always automatically eliminates all unused code, regardless of the imported module's format
Tree-shaking only works with TypeScript, never with plain JavaScript

quiz.question: Why is code splitting (splitting into several bundles) useful as a complement to classic bundling?
options: It allows loading only the code needed for the current page or feature, instead of sending a single huge file for the entire application on first load
It's only used to make code harder to read for security reasons
It completely replaces the need to minify code

culture: The massive shift of the JS community toward Vite since 2020-2021 illustrates a recurring cultural phenomenon in the ecosystem: a new tool that fixes the perceived slowness of a dominant tool (here Webpack, long the absolute standard) can shift adoption across an entire industry very quickly, sometimes within just a few years.

pionnier.portrait: Developer who created Vue.js in 2014, then Vite, released in 2020, after previously working at Google on experimental UI-related projects.
pionnier.contribution: He designed Vite, a build tool that rethinks the development experience by relying on the browser's native ES modules rather than a full bundling step on every startup.
pionnier.problematique: On large projects, traditional bundlers like Webpack were becoming slower and slower to start and refresh during development, since they had to rebundle a large part of the application on every change.
pionnier.solution: He proposed serving source code almost as-is to the browser via native ES module imports during development, only truly bundling at production build time (via esbuild then Rollup).
pionnier.resultat: Vite quickly gained massive adoption in the JavaScript ecosystem after 2020, pushing many existing frameworks and projects to adopt it as their default build tool instead of Webpack.

ambiguite.question: Does Vite completely eliminate the need to bundle code?
ambiguite.reponse: No, only during DEVELOPMENT (where it serves modules almost as-is to the browser). At final BUILD time for production, Vite does indeed bundle the code (via esbuild then Rollup) — the confusion comes from the fact that this bundling is invisible and deferred while you're developing.
